claims.claim_text: Wallach holds a dual stance on fluorine/fluoride. On the other hand he treats water fluoridation as highly controversial and links it to cancer. Following 1977 epidemiological studies by Yiamouyiannis and Burk, full-scale congressional hearings examined the charge that 10,000 excess cancer deaths were caused by fluoridating certain public water systems. The resulting U.S. National Toxicology Program animal study, reported in 1990, found increased precancerous lesions and squamous-cell carcinoma of the oral mucous membranes, a rare osteosarcoma (bone cancer) at double the rate in males as females, and a significant increase in thyroid follicular-cell tumors and liver cancer. Clinical fluoride toxicity appears as dental fluorosis at 2 to 7 parts-per-million and osteosclerosis at 8 to 20 parts-per-million, with chronic systemic toxicity at 20 to 80 milligrams per day over years; the average American already takes in about 4.4 milligrams per day from food, toothpaste, supplements and water.

Iron deficiency arises from unsupplemented pregnancy, menstruation, chronic infection, hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid from salt-restricted diets or proton-pump inhibitors), chronic diarrhea, chronic bleeding, and impaired absorption from high-fat or high-phytate diets and gluten intolerance. Its symptoms include listlessness, fatigue, heart palpitations on exertion, rapid pulse (tachycardia), reduced cognition and memory, sore tongue, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and hypochromic microcytic anemia. Stomach hydrochloric acid and vitamin C aid absorption; heme iron from meat is 10 percent absorbable versus 1 percent from plants (phytates bind it). He notes excess iron storage can be caused by deficiencies of selenium, copper or zinc and is falsely blamed for liver cirrhosis, pancreatic fibrosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

Wallach states that classic protein (nitrogen) deficiency results in infertility, poor growth, lowered immune status, edema, and Kwashiorkor -- the potbellied, thin children of third-world countries. Because the availability and usability of nitrogen differs greatly between foods, protein sources must be chosen with that in mind.

Wallach explains that 'salt hunger' is one of the most basic cravings of animals and man, strongest in herbivores and human vegetarians because grains, vegetables and fruit contain little sodium chloride. Addison's disease (failure of the adrenal cortex) causes a loss of sodium and potassium retention with general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss and a marked salt hunger, relieved by salt supplementation. Sodium-chloride deficiency arises mainly in hot weather or heavy exercise with profuse sweating; Wallach warns that 'water intoxication' killed infants fed low-sodium formulas -- their brains swelled from a simple sodium deficiency -- and that the treatment for sodium deficiency is water and salt, taken orally or as 0.9% intravenous saline.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's answer is nuanced, not a blanket 'avoid fish.' The mercury in fish is methyl mercury, and it bioaccumulates the more fish you eat — the real offenders being the large predator fish: shark, tuna, and swordfish. He lays the body-burden out in plain tiers: people who rarely eat fish carry very little mercury (about 2-5 ug/kg), moderate eaters sit 10 ug/kg, and heavy eaters of those big predators can climb to 400 ug/kg — on the order of 100 times the occasional eater. So the caution is aimed at loading up on the large predators, not at fish generally. Wallach also points to the protection built into his own framework: selenium and mercury are mutual antagonists, so keeping selenium adequate defends the body against the mercury it does take in.
